nameStory: The 'Stretched Jellyskin' gets its name from its thin, membrane-like appearance that looks like translucent skin pulled taut over a surface. When wet, it becomes gelatinous and jelly-like, swelling up like a soft cushion that you could almost imagine poking with your finger. The 'stretched' part refers to how the lichen forms thin, smooth sheets that seem to be pulled across the bark or rock where it grows.
description: Stretched Jellyskin is a leafy lichen that forms thin, smooth patches on tree bark and occasionally rocks. It has a distinctive blue-gray to brownish color and a uniquely soft, membrane-like texture that becomes noticeably gelatinous when wet. The patches are typically small, usually just an inch or two across, and lie very flat against their surface like a piece of wet tissue paper. This lichen belongs to a special group called 'jelly lichens' because they contain blue-green algae that make them swell dramatically with moisture.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels remarkably smooth and membrane-like when dry, almost like touching thin leather or parchment paper, but swells into a soft, gelatinous cushion when wet that feels squishy to gentle pressure

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms thin, flat patches that lie tightly against the surface with slightly raised, wrinkled edges that create small ridges and valleys across the surface

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Blue-gray to olive-brown when dry, becoming much darker and more vibrant blue-green or brownish when thoroughly wet

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on smooth bark of deciduous trees, particularly maples and oaks, rarely found on rough-barked trees or rocks

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches typically measure 1-3 inches across, though several patches may grow near each other to cover larger areas

habitat: Stretched Jellyskin prefers the smooth bark of mature deciduous trees in humid forest environments throughout New England's lower elevations. You'll most likely spot it on maple, beech, and oak trees in mixed hardwood forests where there's consistent moisture and some protection from direct sunlight. It thrives in areas with clean air and stable humidity, making it more common in undisturbed woodlands than in urban or heavily polluted areas.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant and noticeable during frequent spring rains when it swells with moisture and displays its characteristic jelly-like texture. Color changes are most dramatic as it alternates between wet and dry states.
seasonality.summer: Often appears dried and inconspicuous during hot, dry periods, looking like thin brownish patches, but quickly revives and swells after summer thunderstorms.
seasonality.fall: Remains visible and responsive to autumn rains and morning dew, with color changes particularly noticeable against the changing foliage backdrop.
seasonality.winter: Stays present on bark throughout winter, swelling during thaws and rain events, though growth is minimal during cold periods.

funFact: This lichen can absorb up to 20 times its dry weight in water and transform from a papery-thin patch into a plump, jelly-like cushion in just minutes during a rainstorm—imagine a tiny natural sponge that inflates like a balloon every time it rains!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other smooth, thin lichens on bark, but the jelly-like swelling when wet is a dead giveaway—if you can gently press it when moist and it feels squishy rather than firm or brittle, you've found a jelly lichen. Remember: 'If it's jelly when wet, you're on the right track.'
contextualKnowledge: The term 'jelly lichen' refers to lichens that contain cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) instead of or in addition to regular green algae, which gives them their unique ability to swell dramatically with water. This group requires very clean air to survive, making them excellent indicators of good environmental quality.
compareHints: Stretched Jellyskin differs from Blue Jellyskin by being thinner and more tightly attached to bark, while Blue Jellyskin tends to have more pronounced lobes that lift away from the surface. Unlike other Leptogium species in New England, Stretched Jellyskin has a distinctly granular surface texture (hence 'milligranum' meaning small grains) that's visible with a hand lens, giving it a slightly bumpy feel even when the overall surface appears smooth.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Blue Jellyskin differs from its Jellyskin relatives by its distinctive blue color when wet—other species in the genus tend to turn brown, olive, or dark green when moist.
**[UNCERTAIN]** Compared to the more common Blue Jellyskin in the same genus, Leptogium laceroides appears to have more fragmented, irregularly torn lobe margins and may be overall smaller in size.
Unlike Blue Jellyskin which has a more distinctly bluish cast when wet, this species tends toward brownish-gray tones.
